message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What the law says | Practical Tips | |----------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (repairs, cleaning, unpaid rent). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs and deduct from rent (but do so carefully). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend all court hearings. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, receipts). | • Document the issue and your attempts to get it fixed. | | **Subletting** | • The lease may prohibit subletting; if it does, you need the landlord’s written permission. | • Get written consent before subletting. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in writing. | | **Tenant Insurance** | • Texas law does not require renters’ insurance, but it’s highly recommended to protect personal property. | • Shop for a policy that covers theft, fire, and liability. | | **Legal Resources** | • **Texas Attorney General’s Office** – consumer protection.
• **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – discrimination complaints.
• **Local tenant‑rights groups** (e.g., Texas Tenants Union). | • Contact these agencies if you need help. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask for a written copy** of any verbal agreements. 3. **Verify the landlord’s identity** and ownership of the property. 4. **Document the unit’s condition** with photos and a move‑in checklist. 5. **Confirm utility responsibilities** and any required insurance. ### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Send a written notice (email/text) and keep a copy | If no response, consider withholding rent or filing a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office | | Unreasonable late fee | Review lease terms; if fee is excessive, negotiate or refuse to pay | File a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office | | Discrimination | Document incidents; file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD | | Eviction notice | Respond in writing; attend the court hearing | Seek legal aid or representation | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely notice before entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for ending a lease or contesting an eviction. Keep thorough records, communicate in writing, and know where to seek help if your landlord violates your rights.
